Latest Update: Research Notes Cold Muscles Produce Less Power. Here’s How to Protect Your Performance on Frigid Runs.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop.
  • According to recent reports, but what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction?
  • It has been revealed that A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop. Both the research and anyone who’s put in miles on a hot summer afternoon can confidently tell you that much.

According to recent reports, but what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction? Does colder weather in the winter—ranging from just a bit chilly to downright frigid—take a toll on your running too?

It has been revealed that A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does. According to the study’s authors, when our muscles get too cold, neuromuscular function becomes impaired. On the run, this can contribute to stiffness, less power output, and decreased endurance, all of which may cause your winter workouts to feel harder than usual.

Recent findings suggest that the good news? You can still run strong when the temps drop—as long as you make a few key training adjustments before, during, and after you log your miles in the colder months of the year. Here’s how to do just that.

There’s no exact number on the thermometer at which runners can universally expect their power, speed, or endurance to decline, Stephen Cheung, PhD, the lead author of the aforementioned review, tells Runner’s World.

Temperature is just one of the many factors that contribute to how well we perform in the cold, Cheung explains. “It’s a function of the environment, as well as how much heat you’re generating, the speed that you’re moving at, and of course, the amount of clothing that you’re wearing,” he indicates.

Each of these factors varies significantly from runner to runner and affects how quickly their bodies lose heat. You only need to consider those in your run group who run shirtless when it’s freezing versus those who bundle up when it’s 50 degrees Fahrenheit to understand that we all thermoregulate (maintain our internal body temperature) differently. And the equation only becomes more complex when you account for wind and moisture—both in the environment and what you create yourself from air resistance and sweat.

It has been revealed that heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, agrees. “It would be great to be able to say, when the temperature outside reaches [a certain point], your pace slows down by this many seconds per mile—but that’s not how it works,” she says.

Keeping this in mind, Milton states the cleanest reference point for runners to begin paying more attention to how they prepare for runs in the cold is when the temperature drops below freezing. Generally speaking, the colder it gets from there, the more noticeable the negative effects on performance will be, she explains.

It has been revealed that cold weather leads to vasoconstriction, Milton explains, which means our blood vessels constrict more, so the muscles farther away from the core don’t receive as much blood flow. If your fingers or toes have ever gone numb in the cold, for example, you’ve experienced the joy of vasoconstriction. Our bodies prioritize heating our core over our extremities because it helps our vital organs maintain a consistent temperature, which is essential for survival in dangerous conditions.

This physiological response, however, doesn’t bode especially well for running performance.

In a recent development, “The cold slows nerve conduction so you have to work harder for the same power output,” Milton says. “And as temperatures drop further below freezing, that slower nerve conduction and the effects of vasoconstriction are going to be even more noticeable.” As a result, your overall exercise capacity decreases, meaning you may not be able to run for as long or at the same pace you normally would.

What else might you notice when temperatures drop? “Physically, if your muscles and tendons are cold, they’re going to be tighter, less elastic, and you won’t be able to contract them as strongly,” indicates Cheung. “Stiff muscles can also put you at greater risk for tears or strain injuries.”.

Milton states this analogy, used by an old coach of hers, provides an easy way to understand what’s happening: When your muscles and tendons get too cold, they’re like a cold rubber band that can snap when pulled.

In a recent development, if you’re a runner who dislikes the cold, you might wonder if the smarter choice is to just run on the treadmill this winter. Don’t worry: As long as you prepare appropriately and use caution, you can absolutely continue logging regular miles outdoors.

It has been revealed that running well outside in the cold starts with warming up indoors first, says Milton. “An indoor warmup increases your internal metabolism and enhances blood flow, which helps prepare your muscles for contraction,” she explains. This also produces heat so your internal body temperature is more resilient to the cold outdoor environment.

Your winter warmup does not have to be any different or longer than your usual routine, Milton notes. But you do want to make sure that you’re getting in a solid five minutes of prerun drills to adequately raise your body temperature and activate your muscles.

In a recent development, she recommends starting with slower, more controlled movements that help activate the core and the glutes, such as planks with leg raises, lunges with rotation, and hip CARs (controlled articular rotations). Finish with quicker drills that require your nerves to fire more rapidly, such as leg swings and butt kicks.

Equally important to warming up is layering up—with an important caveat.

In a recent development, when dressing for winter runs, keep in mind how you personally respond to cold temperatures, says Cheung, because everyone has different tolerances and susceptibilities. “I get very cold in my hands, so I’ll wear really thick gloves, even when I may be wearing relatively little on my torso,” he adds. “Pay attention to what’s an problem for you and adapt your clothing to both the conditions and your own peculiarities.” Cheung emphasizes this because you don’t want to end up sweating too heavily, which can then leave you chilled and clammy.

Sources indicate that if you need a starting point for your winter running wardrobe, aim for two to three layers of breathable, moisture-wicking fabrics. If possible, choose a wind- and water-resistant shell for your outermost layer, suggests Milton. For your lower body, wear shorts over your tights to help keep your glutes warm. Finally, cover any exposed skin on your head, ears, and hands, and opt for a pair of wool socks—all of which can help ensure adequate blood distribution to the extremities, Milton adds.

When you head out for runs in the cold, slowly build up to your usual pace.

Gradually easing into your workout gives your muscles more time to adjust, and it can also help your airways get used to the colder temperatures, Milton says. You don’t necessarily need to go slower for your entire run, but you should try to match your rate of perceived exertion (RPE) with your typical effort, rather than aiming for your usual pace or heart-rate zone.

According to recent reports, “Think about it the same way as if you were running on an extremely hot day,” Milton claims. “Let’s say your RPE for an easy run is about 3 out of 10. Keep that 3 out of 10, even if your pace is a little slower.”.

Industry observers note that if you find that your run feels more difficult than usual, slow down if you need to, but don’t stop completely, Cheung advises. “Don’t take long breaks, because that’s when you aren’t generating as much heat. Just keep moving so you have that constant heat generation,” he notes.

It has been revealed that if you start to get cold on a run, try speeding up a little bit to stoke that metabolic heat production, Cheung says. But make sure you do it safely: Don’t force the effort in icy conditions or when your muscles feel especially stiff. Scouting out run routes with more tree coverage to block wind on blustery days can also help you stay warmer, he adds.

As soon as you finish your workout, change out of your sweaty running gear and into warm, dry clothes, Milton says.

Even if you’ve only sweated a small amount—for example, maybe you just have some dampness under your armpits—you still want to remove any wet fabrics against your skin. “Even that small amount of wetness can start to drop your core temperature,” Milton explains. If you wait until you’re near shivering, you’ll face an uphill battle to get yourself warm again.

You can also opt for a relaxing shower and hot chocolate—extra marshmallows.

Industry observers note that morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#126490. An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3997 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running.
  • In a recent development, karen took up running in the years after she lost her world.
  • In a recent development, erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story was originally published in June 2021.

There are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.

In a recent development, karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.

In a recent development, erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.

Industry observers note that karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she says. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.

She thinks about Reagan and Grant.

On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that proposal, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.

The trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.

On the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.

Recent findings suggest that he’s killing my kids, she mentioned, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.

Her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? Why didn’t she race to her car and drive 190 miles an hour to reach them? She can’t explain. She only kept rocking back and forth, back and forth. The next thing she remembers is her uncle walking through the front door. He kneeled beside her and whispered in her ear, “They’re gone.”.

Industry observers note that it was her best friend, Brandy, who got her running. Brandy was once a lost teenager who shot up heroin; now she’d become a sober woman who found release through her body in motion, and she wanted Karen to find it too.

In a recent development, she did, but often it felt like anguish. She muttered and cussed and yelled. This is stupid. It hurts. Why am I doing this? Karen didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer. She ran a half marathon less than a year after the tragedy, a full marathon the next.

Still, the grief escalated. The shock and adrenaline wore off after two years, leaving a fathomless despair. One night in May 2018, she laid out hydrocodone, Valium, and Xanax. The plan was to wash them down with vodka and wine and not wake up.

In a recent development, her memory of that night is spotty, but she remembers looking at a picture of Reagan and Grant. She was desperate, sobbing. She did not want to die, but she could not understand what she was doing on Earth without them. I need you to intervene, she begged them. Soon after, she remembers getting a text from a cousin checking in on her, then another cousin, then a friend, then her sister. Karen took it as a sign. She threw away the pills.

Industry observers note that two weeks later, her father checked her into a residential treatment center outside Nashville that specialized in trauma. It was a serene place, acres of rolling pasture, and Karen spent hours on the wooded trail out back, running. Some people who lose their children don’t make it. Alcohol and drugs take them; the suicide rate is higher than average. Eventually Karen came to accept that if she died, then Reagan and Grant died with her, and she couldn’t let them die twice.

In a recent development, she discovered the trail at Erwin Park after returning home to North Texas. Over the next two years her race distances ramped up quickly, from 50 miles to 100K. Karen, who had once made fun of Brandy’s cracked and blistered feet, was now the one peeling off toenails, running her fingers over the watery bubble of a blister. The fifth anniversary of her children’s death was the first time she ran 100 miles. As the hours went by, she checked her watch, trying to place each of her children’s last moments. This is when he was pouring the gas, this is when he texted.

It has been revealed that she could feel Reagan and Grant on that trail. She always does. A cardinal fluttering past, a heart shape in the stumps of the trees, a pair of blue jays—they’re reminders that although she lost her children, they are with her still. Reagan and Grant are the reasons to keep going—not just over the 100 miles, but in the life she is still figuring out how to live.

Recent findings suggest that karen Sparks had a different life once. She was 25 when she met David Small at the mortgage manufacturer where they worked. A clean, good-looking man, a real charmer. He was eight years older. She liked the salt-and-pepper hair, the goatee. She was wearing pink corduroy pants and a floral top that day; he complimented the outfit. Karen needed compliments. Ever since adolescence—the glasses, the braces—she’d struggled with a sense that she was not pretty enough, not thin enough. Not enough.

In a recent development, karen already had a boyfriend and kept a photo of him at her desk. “He won’t be that for long,” David told her. “I’ll have you.” She laughed, because obviously that was a joke. A bit arrogant, too, though she liked the feeling of being coveted. He was smirking, a micro-movement that struck her then as benign.

To understand why Karen fell so hard for David Small, it helps to understand how badly she wanted to escape. Garden-variety teenage rebellion had escalated fast. She’d been a cheerleader and athlete, the daughter of a charismatic high school football coach who became the principal, but in her 20s, she watched Brandy rope off her arm with a rubber tube and plunge a needle into a vein. Around that time, Karen was arrested for drunk driving. She knew she needed to find a better path.

And she did, but she didn’t. She traded the nice boyfriend for the charming bad boy at the office. She’d dropped out of college, which was probably a mistake, and the working world had been a series of dull cubicle gigs. More than anything, she wanted a family. She wanted to be a wife and a stay-at-home mother. Motherhood felt like a purpose. She’d never been a star student or athlete, but she had heart. She was the kid on the team who got the “hardest worker” award. And maybe because her own father had been so powerful, she believed that marrying David could give her those things.

Her mother didn’t like the guy, but Karen’s father urged his wife to give him the benefit of the doubt. Duke Sparks is a Santa Claus of a man, big laugh, big smile. The eldest of 10, with an alcoholic dad, he raised his siblings. Maybe his mistake—he thinks about this all the time—is that he couldn’t stop saving his daughter. Whatever she wanted, he gave it to her, so when she fell for this man, he wasn’t going to stand in her way. When she asked for the fairy-tale wedding, he gave it to her, even though $30,000 was a chunk of change for a school administrator and his schoolteacher wife.

She bought the gown at one of those significant bridal warehouses. Silver-ivory beads embroidered on the straight corset, a long flowy bottom like a princess at a ball. She took bridal photos in front of black-eyed Susans at a Dallas park that was popular with brides-to-be. She sits on the lawn with a tiara nestled in her brown beachy waves, the diamond ring with three bands fitting together like interlocking puzzle pieces conspicuous on her finger as she rests her cheek in her palm. Karen doesn’t recognize the 27-year-old woman in that picture. It’s like she’s wearing a mask.

In a recent development, the newlyweds moved to a one-story in McKinney, about a half hour north of Dallas, and then a two-story a little farther north in the small town of Van Alstyne. In 2006 she had a baby girl named Reagan, and 17 months later a baby boy named Grant, and the way those two came into the world was the way they walked through it: Reagan swift and bold, Grant taking his time, circumspect. Reagan was Karen’s mini-me. The girl of a thousand smiles, with a smattering of freckles. She was a gymnast who loved to climb the walls, climb the refrigerator, climb anything. The summer before the fire, Reagan learned the backstroke and Grant had just gotten comfortable in the pool. Out on the field, though, he was a heck of a ballplayer. He was very particular about his clothes—everything had to match—and had a thing for neons. Those two loved tricking their grandfather into eating Sour Patch Kids. They’d promise him the candy wasn’t sour—definitely not sour, no way was it sour—then when he popped one into his mouth and his face puckered, they’d fall to the floor laughing. They were happy kids. The marriage was rocky, surely they heard things, but Karen is pretty sure they were happy.

It has been revealed that david had trouble keeping a job, though. He had trouble keeping the electricity on, keeping the mortgage paid. In a word, he had trouble. He pawned her ring shortly after Grant was born. Karen sat on the steps of their lease-to-own home, weeping. How could this happen? We have to make sacrifices, that’s what he remarked. He promised it would never happen again, but it just kept happening. Karen’s credit card started getting declined. David once bought the kids scooters for Christmas, only to pawn them. He kept the car parked in the back to keep it from repo men.

After the fire, Karen visited the house. She had to retrace the steps, witness the damage with her own eyes. She pulled back the canvas that investigators had draped over the carpet in the master bathroom. She had to see it: The silhouettes of her children’s bodies, soot outlining their final positions like sidewalk chalk. Some mothers never want to go back, she gets it, but she needed this. What also stands out from that visit is the enormous engagement photo of her in that wedding dress. Flames had licked the canvas, so the picture-perfect image had crackled and turned blister-black.

Why did you stay? Karen could torture herself with this until the end of time if she wanted to. Did you ever think he was capable of such wickedness? Of course not! He never hit her. He never hit the children, never even threatened it. No drinking problem, no drug addiction, no gambling, as far as she can tell. But when Karen scans for warning signs, she thinks about his charm. The subtle manipulation, gaslighting, coercion. How many serial killers, how many con men, how many two-bit criminals get described this way by some innocent bystander? He was so nice, so good-looking, so charming. David’s favorite movies were The Talented Mister Ripley and Catch Me if You Can. So yeah, that was a clue.

It has been revealed that some signs were more obvious, especially to people who weren’t Karen. Her sister trailed him twice to see if he was going to work. (He wasn’t.) Though their memories of the incident are foggy, Karen remembers that her sister tried to show her a photo of him meeting another woman. Karen couldn’t hear it. David loved her. He loved their kids. Karen had gone on antidepressants for postpartum depression after Grant was born, and she wonders if the meds kept her hazy.

In a recent development, also, Karen did not quit things. The little girl who got “hardest worker” trophies would not give up on her marriage so easily. Resilience would be her strength, and her undoing.

It was her father who finally convinced her to leave. Duke had run a background check and found David had an outstanding arrest warrant for unpaid traffic tickets. He called his daughter from the football field. He’s driving around with your kids, he told her. If they arrest him, they’re taking those kids to social services.

Industry observers note that that startled Karen. Reagan was 9. Grant was 8. Her instinct to protect them overrode any fear of leaving.

Industry observers note that she pulled David into the bathroom one night so they could talk in private. The bathroom had a worn brown carpet that led to a walk-in closet. She leaned against the countertop with the double sink and spoke in a voice more defeated than angry. This was over. No fighting. His voice was calm, too. I’m sorry, baby. I’ll fix it, baby.

The fire began in the garage. He’d poured gasoline through the house, dousing the walls, dousing the furniture. The investigators had never seen so much gas. The children lay on the carpet inside the master bathroom where he and Karen had stood just a month before, when she’d told him it was over.

Recent findings suggest that how he kept the kids compliant is a mystery. No drugs were found in their system, no sign of struggle. The children were arranged the way they usually slept, Reagan on her side, Grant on his tummy. David’s body was curled in a ball at the back of the closet, holding down one of the dogs. That sorry coward had placed his kids closest to the flame.

Industry observers note that karen had finally left him on October 19. Her attorney had recommended that she go without warning, so she moved the kids to her parents’ place. After David was served divorce papers, he told her he didn’t see it coming. He just didn’t think his wife would do this.

“You got me,” he texted her that day.

She shot back, “I learn from the best.”.

Industry observers note that halloween had been his first weekend alone with the kids. Karen saw no reason to punish him, even though he seemed to be punishing her. He took Reagan and Grant trick-or-treating, but he didn’t send one photo to Karen of them in their costumes.

Sources indicate that then came Sunday, November 1, 2015. He started texting her at 6 a.m. Are you coming to church with us?

It has been revealed that was he kidding? No, she wasn’t going to church with them. She wasn’t playing “happy family” anymore.

Industry observers note that the texts kept coming, all morning long. I need to talk to you. There’s something I need to tell you. Her family told her to ignore him. Do not go back, it’s a trap. Karen had gone back so many times. She stayed firm. The texts stopped around noon.

Her mind runs alternate scenarios of what might have happened if she’d gone that day, and though she’ll never know, she believes he would have killed her. She thinks he wanted to take them all down together. Instead, he took her children, the pets, most of her belongings, her unshakable faith in God, nearly everything she had, and left her the lone survivor.

According to recent reports, from what Karen can piece together, it seems his blueprint was to blow up the house, leaving nothing but ashes. But the trail of fire never reached the master bathroom. The bodies did not burn. Cause of death, carbon monoxide poisoning and smoke inhalation. Karen hates the phrase “at least”—at least you got them for nine years, at least you were a mother for a while—but this part really is an at least. He’d left a suicide note. Some nonsense about seeing her in heaven. How long had he been plotting this? Some answers she’ll never get.

Was he unstable? Clearly. Narcissistic sociopath turned psychopath, that’s her best guess. Karen has spent the past five-plus years puzzling out the question of why, and she hasn’t gotten far. Part of her trauma therapy at the treatment center was reenacting that day, placing herself in the scene she never entered in real life, a technique known as psychodrama. The benefit was profound, but it never gave her the “why.” There is no word in the English language for a mother who loses her children, the way there is for widows and orphans. It’s like language itself cannot admit the possibility.

Sources indicate that the fourth year was even harder than the first three. Grief kept amplifying. She got tattoos. Their names on her outer left forearm. Their birth dates in Roman numerals on her inner right wrist. Angel wings on her ankles, which she got with another mother who’d lost her kids. And on the tender ivory of her inner bicep, the phrase that has become her motto: Love never ends. She dyed her hair magenta and started painting her nails in bright neons. The look is a bit out there for a 43-year-old woman in small-town Texas, but the wildness fits her soul, and she likes to think her kids are proud. She believes they see her the same way she sees them.

On November 1, 2020, Karen ran the 100 miles by herself, but she wasn’t alone. People had flocked to support her. One woman ran alongside her for 50 miles. Another flew in from Indiana to crew. Karen didn’t even know some of these people. But they had heard her story and wanted to help. At pit stops, her coach and his wife massaged her feet. It felt nearly Biblical. Her feet. Her dad was there from beginning to end, sleeping in his truck at night.

Karen had never seen a pit crew hustle so hard; it felt like NASCAR. They changed her clothes, popped her blisters, fed her when her stomach could take it. Pringles, PB&J sandwiches, ice-cold Coca-Cola. Her favorite was mashed potatoes and ramen. Sounds disgusting, but it went down smooth and easy as night fell.

In a recent development, somewhere in the dark, she started to hallucinate. The trees came alive. They turned into fairyland creatures, with swooping limbs and kind faces. Karen was Little Red Riding Hood, running from the Significant Bad Wolf. She was Katniss Everdeen, an ordinary girl who never asked to be a hero. The sun came up, she scarfed down pancakes and syrup, and she could see the faces of the people who showed up for her, and the feeling was golden.

Around mile 70, she started to crumble. She broke down when she briefly couldn’t find her dad at the pit stop. Duke wondered if it was time for his daughter to call it quits, but he knew her better than that. She would crawl to the end if she had to, but she would finish.

It took Karen 31 hours to complete the run, an hour longer than planned. She beat herself up about the extra time until her team reminded her that what she’d done was harder than most races, not just because of the personal stakes but because she couldn’t feed off the energy of other runners, spectators, all those passing people. Even Karen had to admit: One woman, 100 miles. It was a triumph.

Karen had never wanted this. She only wanted to be a mom. But this loss summoned a strength she didn’t know she had. Back in her previous life, she did not have the courage to stand on her own. This part is confusing, it fills her eyes with tears, because losing Reagan and Grant was the worst thing that had ever happened to her—but it also made her more like the woman she wanted to be.

Sources indicate that she’s working on a memoir with her sister, and she prepares to keep racing. Another 100-miler in October, a 200-miler after that; her dream is the Moab 240. Reminders of her loss never go away. Kids playing on a jungle gym. An empty swing. The memories can bring a smile, or they can bring a tear. She has learned to live with both: happy and sad, furious and grateful, lucky and cursed. Sixty-eight months. That’s how long it’s been since her world split open. Every first day of the month marks another notch in that marathon.

Most people want to outrun emotional pain. Not Karen. She runs into the pain. “Run toward the roar” is a line she read in a book about grief, and it’s why she can tell this story to a stranger in a cozy cafe, because she’s learned that sharing the pain is a better path. Allowing herself to be angry and difficult and complicated and hurt, swiping away tears and muttering cuss words only to apologize because she knows this is for a magazine—that’s better than pretending.

In a recent development, it will tell you about her spirit, and the radiance of this woman who never asked for any of this, that as she tells the worst story of her life, a man stops to comment on her smile. Another man stops, an hour later, to compliment her hot pink nails. In other parts of the world, and to other women, such comments might not go over well, but Karen flashes that smile. “It’s them,” she states, finger pointing upward, and maybe that’s true. It’s also true her smile was here before they were. And though she will never stop running for Reagan and Grant, maybe one day she will run for herself. It’s the next step.

New Balance SC Elite V5 + FuelCell Rebel V5 Running Shoes.

Industry observers note that black Friday sales are notorious for flooding inboxes with endless discounts on triathlon gear you might not actually need. Triathlete’s editors are no exception: for the past two months, they have received a deluge of notifications teasing Black Friday deals from just about every triathlon brand.

Sources indicate that but our staff, who test and review gear year-round, know not every sale is worth shopping. After all, what good is a big Black Friday discount on cheap triathlon gear if it requires replacement in a few months?

To separate the signal from the noise, we asked our very own Triathlete editors to share the items sitting in their online shopping carts this holiday season. From reliable daily trainers and high-end smartwatches to cold-weather layers and budget-friendly pool essentials, here are the Black Friday deals our team is actually buying with their own money.

Recent findings suggest that have you ever found that pair of shoes where it was immediate love at first stride? You just knew you’d found yourself in a new, long-term relationship, and for the next several weeks, you were in the honeymoon phase – enjoying running more and convincing yourself that running in carbon shoes was fine because this was the only shoe you wanted to run in. Forever.

That was me with the Latest Balance SC Elite V4. That might surprise a few people, as it’s not the fastest or flashiest of shoes – and very few pros wore it. Yet it just ticked all the boxes: a wide toe box, stable, grippy, and breathable. They’re the not-intimidating super shoe I recommend to everyone looking to try super shoes. And to top it off, they lasted two seasons and far more miles than you’re ever supposed to put on them.

That’s why the SC Elite V5 is on my shopping list. It’s not only well past time to replace my current pair, but the newly introduced version promises to be lighter and faster, with a couple of small complications, like the short tongue, addressed. Alex Yee and Laura Philipp both wore this shoe to great effect, and now I think it’s my turn.

But I can’t just run in these for every session. Sigh. I must also shop for a daily trainer that matches the love I have for the Elites, and that’s why I’m shopping for the FuelCell Rebel V5. After temporarily trading my trusty Adidas EVO SLs for a friend’s new Rebels for a couple of laps around the track, I was immediately hooked. Again, even though they might not be as popular as the SLs, it’s all about your relationship with the shoe – and I knew I’d just found my next pair of daily trainers.

Sources indicate that with both on sale at Running Warehouse for way less than they deserve, it’s time to stop talking about relationships with shoes and just get them. Otherwise, my wife will say I should just go on dates with them instead.

-Travis Mundell, social media manager.

It has been revealed that I’ve entered the payoff phase of parenting where my oldest son is becoming a fun companion for activities. We’re running our first 5K together in December. While our outerwear will be holiday sweaters, he needs some base layers to stay warm from the December chill.

Backcountry has decent prices on Smartwool’s kids’ base layers, ideal for little ones who will likely outgrow the apparel after just one season (though my 3-year-old has proudly proclaimed she will be running cross “crunchy,” so the base layers will get good use).

Recent findings suggest that while I’m shopping, I’m also going to replace some of my threadbare running socks, which I’ve been avoiding. Smartwool is one of my favorite durable sock brands and they are 25% off.

– Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

As someone who tests a lot of endurance-focused smartwatches (pretty much all of them that have been made in the last decade), I know a good watch — and a good deal on a watch — when I see one.

When the Suunto Race 1 came out in 2023, I reviewed it for Triathlete. At the time, I gave it 4.5 out of 5 stars, only dinging it for a slow raise-to-wake/processor that was slightly behind the competition. Pros included a giant, bright AMOLED touchscreen, excellent offline mapping and a useful rotating digital dial, and shockingly solid battery life for a massive-screened AMOLED smartwatch. The other major pro was what I considered an incredibly thrifty price — $500 at the time for the titanium model with more storage than the even cheaper (and heavier) steel $400 version.

Three years later, I still consider the original Suunto Race a menace to the rest of Suunto’s line: The Race 2 somehow had less battery life than the original, but cost way more; and I don’t even consider the Race 3S a worthy challenger to either of the previous models in function or price.

So now that this fully triathlete-approved smartwatch with a gigantic screen and handy rotating dial (best for navigation) is available at $320 in the Titanium version and a category-shattering $280 for the steel version, you can’t even compare it to those other ill-fated Race models nor other smartwatches like the capable-but-not-nearly-enough-storage-for-offline-mapping (and small-screened) Coros Pace 4 ($250).

In a recent development, and equivalent Garmin models like the Forerunner 570 (on sale for $450 down from $550) can’t even remotely compete on price or battery life. Don’t be turned off by the age of this watch; pick it up now, be satisfied for years, and take the money you save and put it toward some holiday gift-giving.

– Chris Foster, editor-in-chief.

It’s the end of the season, which means two things:.

Naturally, Black Friday serves as the perfect time to bag a few fresh suits and swim necessities. To me, the fresh gear equals a fresh mindset as I enter a swim-focused block of winter training. I live in Arizona, where sunshine and heated pools are abundant, so swimming all winter is something I actually get excited about. Sashaying onto the pool deck in new gear just makes it even more fun.

Recent findings suggest that with that said, I’ll be hitting up the bonkers deal on Arena one-piece swimsuits ($17, down from $75!), as well as picking up a few pairs of 30% off Speedo Fastskin Pure Focus goggles, which received high marks in our 2026 roundup of the best triathlon swim goggles. I’m also picking up this $11 neoprene swim cap from Sporti, because every time I find myself at a cold-weather race, the expo vendors are more than happy to sell me the same product for five times that amount.

And just for funsies, I’ll throw in this $8 swim cap decorated as a crown – because if I’m going to rule lane four this winter, I might as well dress the part.

Before “cloud” was associated with On’s trainers and Phil Knight cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports, which eventually became Nike, there was Asics. The brand was founded over 75 years ago as Onitsuka Tiger, and would eventually merge with the Asics Corporation in 1977. The Asics “tiger stripes” logo on its shoes derives from the 1950s Onitsuka Tiger Mexico 66 shoe model. Its Gel-Cumulus and Gel-Nimbus legacy models were released in 1999.

Industry observers note that though the manufacturer is Japanese, the origin of Asics’s name is actually a Latin acronym, anima sana in corpore sano, for “sound mind in a sound body.” This ethos is exemplified when wearing, running, and racing in an Asics shoe. The brand’s dynamic cushioning provides comfort and a responsive ride for all running experiences. Well-received by wear-testers, we’ve included Asics trainers in multiple buying guides, including Best Running Shoes and the 2026 Shoe Awards.

Runner’s World has offered running advice and gear recommendations since 1966. We assembled a 300-plus-runner local group of varying experience levels, paces, and foot types to test the latest shoe releases and give their honest assessments on fit, comfort, and ride.

Industry observers note that the shoes included on this list were all vetted by wear-testers and RW staff. I have also included my own experience testing some of these models during all kinds of workouts and in a couple of races.

RW contributor Michael Charboneau provided insight on Asics shoe tech and answered frequently asked questions about Asics trainers.

In a recent development, the Novablast 6 gets an injection of fun that is awfully reminiscent of the original. For this upgrade, though, Asics cored out a hole in the forefoot and filled it with A-TPU, a foam that’s bouncier than PEBA. The effect is that the carrier (the bulk of the midsole) delivers a predictable, stable ride, yet the forefoot feels explosive and propulsive. It makes this everyday trainer suitable for days when you want to pick up the pace.

It has been revealed that “The Asics Novablast 6 is a bouncy do-it-all shoe that excels with faster paces,” mentioned tester and Runner’s World Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Compared to other up-tempo daily trainers I’ve tested, like the. Fresh Balance Rebel v5 and Nike Pegasus 42, it has more cushion and a softer feel, yet is still light and bouncier than both.”.

Testers liked the reworked knit upper, improved AsicsGrip rubber outsole, and responsive trampoline pod of FF Turbo Squared foam in the forefoot.

“Cushioning is the strongest feature of this shoe,” said tester Trevor Conde. “The Novablast is a high-cushioned trainer and it delivers on that. The shoe has a bit more give than most of my go-to trainers, with a higher amount of sinking and compact cushioning during the foot strike phase.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

The GT-2000 underwent a makeover with its 14th iteration. Asics has carried these changes over to the GT-2000 15, ensuring the cushioning feels even softer with an added 2 mm of FF Blast Max foam. One tester said they had the same feel as the Hoka Clifton, saying the Asics shoe was just as comfortable.

According to recent reports, the outsole has the same flame-like pods as the previous version for better traction and stability. The GT-2000 15 also has Asics’s 3D Guidance stability system, which involves high sidewalls for a secure fit and a wider platform for support.

“I’ve had the Asics GT-2000 13 and 14 models, and I was just has happy with this pair as I’ve been with the others,” stated tester and overpronator Sophie Kahler. “I found it to be a solid sneaker for a beginner runner like myself who is looking for a mid-price, versatile shoe with good support. I tested it on road, treadmill, and gravel trail at my usual pace around 9:30 to 10:00. I also did a lot of walking in the shoes and found them comfortable for hours.”.

For an even cheaper option, check out the GT-1000 14 ($115), which also has the brand’s 3D Guidance System.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

It has been revealed that the Gel-Cumulus is a long run favorite for its plush, supportive cushioning. It buffers miles of pounding in a surprisingly lightweight package. The shoe’s midsole is FF Blast Max, which promotes soft landings with high rebound. The foam—along with Asics’s PureGel tech—provides arch support for both neutral runners and underpronators.

Sources indicate that “Compared to other daily trainers I have tested, the Asics Gel-Cumulus 28 is a perfect, stable, trainer,” said Caroline Lennon, a heel-striker who trains at 8:30 pace. “I found myself not interested in reaching for any other shoes in this period, no matter whether I was running on the treadmill, trail, or road. They were exceptionally comfortable and I never had any pain, discomfort, or nagging injury crop up in my time with these shoes.

Industry observers note that “They don’t feel flashy, light, responsive and fast,” she continued. “But when I was waking up, and bleary-eyed pulling on my sneakers for a pre-dawn run, they felt like the comforting warm hug my feet wanted. This made a clear difference on longer efforts, where fatigue typically builds up, and allows me to recover more promptly between sessions.”.

Sources indicate that some testers, however, including myself, felt the loudness of the shoe was distracting. When I tested the Superblast 3 on my runs, the pavement slapping was comparable to Nike’s Alphaflys.

According to recent reports, asics has cooked up quite a few proprietary features, and you’ll see many different terms when browsing the company’s running shoe lineup. To help you get more insight into these features, compare models, and find the right shoe, here’s a deeper dive on the main Asics running shoe tech to know.

Industry observers note that this tech consists of a squishy, gel-like substance implanted in the midsole, and it absorbs impact forces for a smoother ride. The latest iteration is PureGel, and it’s formulated to be lighter, softer, and more flexible than previous versions of Gel.

Like other shoemakers, Asics has its own proprietary cushioning, called FlyteFoam (FF). Although it’s based on ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), the traditional running shoe cushioning material, this foam is formulated to be lighter and more resilient than standard EVA. It doesn’t have quite the same springy feel as the other types of FF below, but it works fine for everyday running. It’s used in Asics’s more affordable shoes.

Industry observers note that FF Blast Plus is the next level up. Asics hasn’t released details on the chemistry, but it likely includes olefin block copolymers, which make for a lighter, more flexible and more responsive foam. For a pillowy and springy ride that still holds up to everyday training, FF Blast Plus is the cushioning to go with.

Asics has also released an updated version, called FF Blast Max, that has a lower density, so it’s even softer and bouncier. It gives models a very plush ride. For maximum cushioning that doesn’t sacrifice responsiveness, look for training shoes with FF Blast Max.

Asics’s elite racing shoes have FF Turbo Plus foam. It’s made with polyether block amide (PEBA), an exceptionally light, soft, and bouncy material. The brand took this foam up a notch with the even bouncier FF Turbo Squared. Leap foam, which is made of Aliphatic TPU (A-TPU), is a super foam that’s softer and lighter than FF Turbo Squares. It is used in the brand’s top tier racing shoes. The shoes with this type of cushioning are pricey, but provide excellent shock absorption and springy responsiveness for a smooth, propulsive ride that helps you go fast. For race day, it’s definitely the top choice.

Asics takes a holistic approach to stability in its shoes, with several features working together to support the foot and guide it from landing to toe-off. The latest version of its stability feature-set is called the “4D Guidance System.” The 4D Guidance shoes feature a wide sole, a firm foam layer in midsole under the arch, and a flared sole shape at the heel to create a planted feel while counteracting overpronation, or excessive inward rolling motion in your step.

Industry observers note that some models have an earlier version of the system, called 3D Guidance. It has the same general features as 4D, but lacks the firm arch support foam in the midsole. If you know you need stability shoes, or simply prefer a more guided, supportive design, then you should look for these features.

In a recent development, asics has developed a well-deserved reputation for manufacturing reliable shoes that can hold up through high-mileage training. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus, Gel-Nimbus, and Gel-Kayano have been around for decades (and continuously improved upon in that time), and they’re great picks if you’re looking for everyday trainers.

That said, the brand has also expanded into lightweight, responsive racing shoes and even trail shoes, too.

How do Asics shoes compare to shoes from other brands?

Historically, Asics shoes have been known for using multiple layers of cushioning to create a stable, well-cushioned (and somewhat stiff) ride. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus still exhibit this construction, with a moderate drop and layers of Gel and foam in the midsole for a plush feel that’s great for long runs and training miles.

However, newer shoes in the Asics lineup, like the Novablast, utilize more lightweight, bouncy midsole designs that mirror what other top brands are doing in their premium speedwork and racing shoes.

Has Asics created any key innovations in running shoe tech?

The short answer: Yes, lots of them. Asics has been experimenting with running shoe tech for well over half a century. In 1990, the brand opened the Institute of Sports Science in Kobe, Japan, where the manufacturer conducts materials tests and biomechanical research to fine-tune designs.

According to recent reports, this lab has produced and refined many of Asics’s hallmark technologies, like Gel cushioning and super foams, like FF Leap and FF Turbo Squared. For runners, this means Asics shoes are built with proven designs that can help you meet your goals, from sticking to a training proposal to nabbing a new PR on race day.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

Flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no shortage of fresh cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable.
  • Sources indicate that our editors bring different perspectives to testing.
  • Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no shortage of fresh cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

Sources indicate that our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+.

I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

It has been revealed that that mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Sources indicate that last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

According to recent reports, when I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates quickly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex Pliers Wrench (86 03 180).

Knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

These aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

Despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

Peak Design Mobile Crossbody Multi-Strap.

Sources indicate that as a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

Its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them quickly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

It has been revealed that spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

According to recent reports, the main issue I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

Back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

Now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

So far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Vittoria Corsa Pro Control Tan, 700x42c.

Debuted in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls quickly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT TR.

I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

In nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit challenges. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

Pearl Izumi Pi PRO/BLACK Mesh Jersey.

Industry observers note that at $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

According to recent reports, the fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common issue I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

In a recent development, it’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

The wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

Heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

The sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

Q36.5 Dottore Pro Long Sleeve Jersey.

The Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

Recent findings suggest that the Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full upgrade to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

Same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a big reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an upgrade to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

But even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing highlighted the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

The Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

In a recent development, the straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

Industry observers note that it is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 announced to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

Sources indicate that other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

Recent findings suggest that one of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics.
  • Research reveals just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine.
  • The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Research reveals just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, indicates core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

Industry observers note that to help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in Upcoming York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

Sources indicate that in addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Recent findings suggest that even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun latest ways, but also engage your brain.

How to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

It has been revealed that tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir indicates. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

Sources indicate that how to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

Why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

Recent findings suggest that how to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Industry observers note that why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir claims. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

Industry observers note that how to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

In a recent development, why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

Sources indicate that how to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir states.

In a recent development, how to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

Why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir claims. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

How to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

According to recent reports, mallory Creveling is an ACE-certified personal trainer and RRCA-certified run coach, who also holds certifications in kettlebell training, sports performance, and more. She has more than 15 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition for a wide range of publications, and nearly 10 years of experience as a trainer and fitness instructor. Mallory stays on top of her continuing education in fitness, as well as the latest science in wellness. She has worked with some of the best experts in their medical fields, and regularly interviews researchers, trainers, athletes, and more to find the best advice for readers looking to improve their performance and well-being.
