Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

You wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions. However, whether you’re hunting for deals or seeking out the latest tech, now is the time to buy. With holiday discounts and fresh e-bikes rolling out to dealers and online retailers, plenty of great commuter, cargo, and e-MTB options are out there—at great prices.

Sources indicate that I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in New York City. Plus, I commute daily on an e-bike and ride test dozens of electric bikes each year. Last summer, I even went almost entirely car-free thanks to an electric cargo bike.

Industry observers note that whether you’re choosing your first e-bike, upgrading to a newer model, or adding another electric model to your garage, dozens of great options are available—and our editors and staff have tested many of them. No matter your age, cycling ability, or budget, brands offer electric bikes that meet needs.

Tip for E-Bike Buyers: Don’t overpay for an electric bike, but spend what you can comfortably afford. If an e-bike is fun to ride, you’ll use it more often. It’s more cost-effective to buy an e-bike equipped the way you want it upfront than to upgrade it later. Also, remember: you cannot change an electric bike’s motor system if you decide you want more power.

Sources indicate that the Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. Over several years, the Level platform has proven to be reliable and low-maintenance. Plus, its price doesn’t break the bank.

Aventon split the 4th-generation Level into two models. The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. Aventon also added regenerative braking, increasing the bike’s range up to 75 miles. The pricier ADV edition features a mid-drive motor; it bumps up the torque to 100 Nm and range to 110 miles. Both versions come standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Another feature consumers will find quite useful is the Level’s connected features. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

BUY LEVEL 4 STEP-THROUGH BUY LEVEL 4 ADV.

The relatively affordable seven-speed model Soltera 2.5 from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat. This makes it an excellent choice for getting around town or quick commutes. It’s even better than the original version, thanks to hydraulic disc brakes. A push of the throttle gets you started; then, the brushless hub motor gently assists your pedaling.

Along with disc brakes, the Soltera features integrated lights and turn signals, and the battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (rather than the bolt-on batteries found on many similarly-priced e-bikes). Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a strikingly light 46-pound package.

Aventon also offers a singlespeed, Soltera 3 ADV with a Gates belt-drive system.

According to recent reports, when buying a low-priced e-bike, a simple, low-cost, easy-to-repair, and reliable model usually beats out complicated designs. Lectric’s XP Lite2 is about as basic as it gets. It has a low-maintenance singlespeed drivetrain, a 300-watt hub motor, and a 375Wh battery. With its compact size, 20x2.5-inch tires, and twist-grip throttle, the XP Lite is perfect for zipping through traffic, commuting to the office, or heading to the gym or bar after work.

According to recent reports, the XP Lite2 features only one gear and a 300W motor, so it’s not ideal for very hilly terrain. But with the throttle, you can get over small rises and bridges. Lectric also equips the bike with hydraulic disc brakes and front and rear lights. The XP Lite2 is also great for RVers and campgrounds, since it’s lightweight (about 48 pounds) and folds down to 36x16x27-inch dimensions.

Many “step-through” e-bikes don’t actually have a low step design. This makes it challenging for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, by REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. The CTY is a great choice for older riders, those with reduced mobility, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

Sources indicate that REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor that provides smooth pedal-assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem for a comfortable riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for better stopping. For less than the cost of some e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI warranty and service.

The Current ADV is the priciest bike in this story, but for a good reason. Some electric bikes look a lot like mountain bikes, but that doesn’t mean they are built for real off-road use. Aventon’s new Current is the brand’s first full suspension E-MTB, and it is trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, mentioned, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers.”.

The Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor with 750 peak Watts and 110 Nm of torque. (It also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and 120 Nm of torque.) Rounding out the ADV are high-end components like a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

Industry observers note that in his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab particularly likes the Current’s easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data as well as the ability to tune the motor settings. If you don’t need rear suspension, check out Aventon’s updated Ramblas ADV hardtail E-MTB.

READ AVENTON CURRENT REVIEWMORE GREAT E-MTBs.

Getting into E-MTB trail riding on a budget is tough. Low-priced electric mountain bikes often aren’t built strong enough for off-road riding (or weigh half a rider’s weight), and trail-capable models typically cost more than $4,000. That’s what makes the TrailRush a standout bike—for less than $2,000, you get a trail-ready hardtail you can take on singletrack and have some fun.

Recent findings suggest that ride1Up equips the 29-inch-wheeled TrailRush with a Brose mid-drive motor. With 90 Nm of torque, it isn’t as powerful as many latest, higher-priced E-MTB motors, but it gets the job done. The TrailRush also comes stock with a dropper seatpost, four-piston disc brakes, and tubeless-compatible rims with Maxxis Minion tires.

Of course, to hit this great price, Ride1Up made some equipment sacrifices. The 504Wh battery isn’t as large as some peers (like the Aventon Ramblas), so you get less ride time between charges. Additionally, the 11-36T cassette and 38T chainring limit your ability to climb steep hills.

It has been revealed that compared to earlier iterations of the Aventure, the third-generation model has a smoother ride and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s fresh torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found earlier models had too much torque, but this Aventure remedied that fault. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-roading, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths, but with this burly bike’s weight and components, it has limited functionality on singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers the Aventure M, a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same massive, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price. Those refinements cost about $1,000 more than the Aventure 3.

In a recent development, buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have limited mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike technology, but it lets you get out and enjoy some rides without breaking the bank.

I combed through dozens of Amazon listings comparing low-priced electric bikes, and this Heybike stood out for its combination of price and features. Then, I saw someone on the local bike path with one and asked them about the bike. The rider liked it and said it has been trouble-free (they noted a local bike shop assembled it for them). Heybike’s U.S. support line is available for warranty service or product questions.

In a recent development, don’t want to purchase from Amazon? Use this exclusive Bicycling discount link for $100 (applied at checkout) off the Cityscape 2.0, plus free shipping.

According to recent reports, tern’s cargo bikes are the gold standard for practical features, durability, and ride quality. This reputation makes the brand’s GSD (longtail) and HSD (short-tail) cargo models top picks for bike commuters, families, and riders looking to cut their dependence on automobiles.

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

According to recent reports, while it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example of this is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

Sources indicate that many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. At the moment priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it boasts an impressive 60-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. (The dual-battery model for $1,799 doubles the range to 120 miles.) This makes the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around and a good option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

According to recent reports, “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, mentioned Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, to reach a price like this, concessions have to be made somewhere. This results in a somewhat cheap feeling to the bike. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but at times, it feels erratic. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend buying.

It has been revealed that plenty of commuter e-bikes cost far less than Specialized’s Turbo Vado SL 2, and they can probably do most of these things. So why spend twice as much as many popular options? I dive into the details in my story, “Stop Wasting Money on Cheap E-Bikes. Here’s Why Spending More Pays Off for Commuters.”.

It has been revealed that the TL;DR: The Turbo Vado SL 2’s excellent ride geometry, silky-smooth motor, low weight, and premium components make riding fun. Together, these features make you want to ride the Vado every day and use it for more than simply getting to work. And thanks to Specialized’s extensive dealer network, you have somewhere to turn when it needs service.

“Lightweight e-bike” might sound like an oxymoron to some, but a sub-40-pound weight is impressive when many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds. And often, e-bikes this light are pricey. Yet, the Velotric Tempo is only $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight.

According to recent reports, velotric achieves this weight reduction by ditching the bulky suspension fork (suspension forks on lower-priced bikes often don’t work all that well, to be frank), swapping heavy tires for 700x42c gravel tires, and using a smaller battery. Riders who need to carry the bike up any stairs or load it onto a bike rack will appreciate the reduced weight. However, heavier riders may want to test ride the Tempo before purchase, as lower-powered motors can bog down and reduce battery range for bigger-bodied people.

Industry observers note that bicycles are my life, and I’m a dedicated e-bike user and enthusiast. I’ve also worked in cycling for over 25 years. For almost six years, I’ve ridden and tested electric bikes as Bicycling’s Deputy Editor—and I use e-bikes for my daily commute. Before joining the staff, I led product development for top bicycle brands.

According to recent reports, our editors test dozens of electric bikes across every cycling category, and we continually receive newly introduced models to evaluate. Our riding involves much more than taking bikes on short spins; we use electric bikes in our daily lives. Commuting, school drop-offs, grocery runs, and daily transportation are only a few of the things we regularly do with e-bikes. We also hit the trails on E-MTB models to test their performance in real-world mountain biking conditions, not simply riding them around town.

Industry observers note that in addition to ride-testing, our editors regularly talk to cyclists of all ages and abilities about their riding needs. This helps us craft our list of Best Electric Bikes: e-bikes that will meet your needs on the street, trails, and around the neighborhood. Two of the e-bikes in this story even made the final cut for our 2026 Bike Awards.

Electric bike prices range from entry-level models for less than $500 to premium machines costing almost as much as a good used car. However, our years of testing have proven that many of the best and most practical models live squarely in the middle.

According to recent reports, we find that many standout e-bikes are priced between $1,500 and $3,000. These models strike a good balance between reliability and practicality, without requiring you to overspend on features or technology you don’t need. Electric bikes costing less than $1,000 often take shortcuts to achieve this, either by using lower-quality parts or offering limited service after the bike is purchased.

Of course, you can also spend much more on electric bikes. Premium e-bikes typically offer improved motor performance, higher-quality components, lower weight, or more tech features. However, for most general riding purposes, these bikes are overkill—but they‘re certainly fun!

Sources indicate that → Consider how much cargo you’ll need to carry if your riding involves commuting or running errands. Look for a bike with appropriate racks, mount points, and other accessories.

→ For singletrack and trail riding, look for mountain bikes with knobby tires, adjustable suspension, high-quality frames, and low weight.

→ Pay attention to weight. While fat tire e-bikes and cargo bikes offer versatility, many weigh over 90 pounds. If you’ll need to carry your bike up any stairs or lift it onto a bike rack, a lighter option will be a better fit.

Sources indicate that → Bike storage is another consideration. While most e-bikes don’t require excessive space compared to their non-pedal-assisted counterparts, ensure you have access to a power outlet where you plan to store it for easy charging.

Several e-bike brands, Aventon, Ride1Up, and Lectric, performed well in our ride testing and evaluations. These bikes might require some minor assembly at home, such as installing pedals, a seat, and tightening handlebars. We considered how easy bikes were to assemble in our recommendations. Many bike shops will not assemble or otherwise work on e-bikes they do not sell due to liability challenges. The direct-to-consumer brands we recommend have dealers nationwide ready to support you.

In a recent development, established bike companies, such as Specialized and Trek, manufacture e-bikes and have hundreds of dealers across North America. Additionally, REI sells its house-brand Co-op electric bikes (and models from Cannondale and Tern) in its stores.

According to recent reports, there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding your bike.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

What this means: Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows consumers to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Other countries classify electric bikes differently, and many do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Electric bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

In a recent development, bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. Mid-drive e-bikes tend to be more expensive, but are typically more reliable and higher performance. Because the extra weight on a mid-drive motor is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors.

Measured in Newton meters (or Nm), torque is a rotational measurement of force—and the number to pay attention to when you want an idea of an e-bike motor’s output. More torque means more power off the line and more boost to your pedaling.

The heavier the bike, the more torque it needs. Lighter road bikes typically have 30 to 40 Nm of torque, and trail and cargo models (generally) have at least 80 Nm. Most commuter bikes fall somewhere in between.

The size of an e-bike’s battery is measured in watt-hours (or Wh). This measurement represents the energy stored in the battery and how many watts it can deliver each hour. The higher the number, the longer the range, but the faster you go, the faster you drain the battery.

So, if a 504Wh battery paired with a 500W motor gives you one hour of ride time at the highest assist, riding at about half that power will double your range.

Many e-bike brands seamlessly integrate batteries to make the bike look sleeker (and more like a traditional non-assist bike). Most batteries lock to the bike and come with a key that lets you unlock and remove it, which serves multiple purposes: You can remove the battery and charge it off the bike, plus a locked battery deters (and hopefully prevents) a thief from stealing it. An e-bike with the battery removed is safer for hauling on a bike rack and lighter for carrying up steps.

Since e-bikes can maintain higher speeds for longer than standard bikes, you want extra control when riding. Wider tires provide better traction and the freedom to leave the pavement with little penalty, and a suspension fork will help tame some of the rougher roads you might explore. Good disc brakes are a must, too, for slowing a heavy bike at high speed. This is not a place to skimp.

Some e-bikes have an integrated lighting system that turns on when you power up the bike. While this is a great feature, it’s not a deal-breaker if your bike doesn’t come equipped this way. It’s just as easy to attach your own since so many great bike lights are available.

E-bikes need regular maintenance and repair to stay in good working condition. Because they’re heavier and go faster than non-assist bicycles, e-bikes often require more regular service on parts like brakes, tires, and drivetrain components. We recommend having a good relationship with a local bike shop experienced in e-bike repair to keep your equipment running smoothly.

E-bikes use electronics for their motors, batteries, and displays. These parts are often proprietary to bike brands or even specific e-bike models, making replacement more difficult than parts on non-electric bicycles. Make sure to use the correct electronic replacement parts to avoid damaging your e-bike (or it catching fire).

Established brands usually (but not always) have a good supply of these parts for replacement, even for years after a bike goes out of production. Bosch and Shimano are two e-bike motor manufacturers with some of the most compatibility between bikes and stock parts for previous generations of systems.

In a recent development, look for e-bikes from brands that offer at least a one-year warranty on electronic components (many brands’ warranties are longer) and make items like replacement batteries for your bike. These parts are usually not cheap (sometimes up to half the cost of a upcoming bike), but it’s the difference between having an e-bike that can be repaired or becomes a bicycle-shaped paperweight if something goes wrong.

In a recent development, following a dramatic increase in fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes, there is a push from local officials, regulatory agencies, and advocacy groups across the U.S. for improved safety certification of e-bikes, batteries, and motor units. In September 2023, a Newly introduced York City law took effect requiring that any e-bike sold in the city “has been certified by an accredited testing laboratory for compliance with Underwriters Laboratories (UL) standard 2849”.

However, just because something is marketed as UL 2849 compliant, tested to UL 2849, or even “certified to UL 2849” does not mean it is UL Safety Certified. Ibrahim Jilani, UL’s Global Director of Consumer Technology, notes: “Certification is always earned by a manufacturer and not a given when they undergo a product submittal. The UL Mark, or any authorized certification mark, can only be issued upon successful demonstration of meeting the requirements of the safety standard.” You can find UL’s updated list of products certified to UL 2849 here. You can cross-reference OSHA’s Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories for a deep dive into the topic.

According to recent reports, as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • They say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running.
  • Recent findings suggest that around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch.
  • Sources indicate that professional distance runner and New York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running. But by “distance,” I don’t mean bumping up my mileage or running farther. I mean taking time and space away from my sport during seasons when I feel burned out, lost, or simply exhausted.

Recent findings suggest that around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch. The second I crossed the finish line, all I wanted to do was let my running shoes collect dust, avoid my local trail, and avoid stepping foot in the gym for a while.

Sources indicate that professional distance runner and New York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago. At that time, she consistently stopped hitting her paces in her workouts and decided to step back from running—a break that lasted about two years.

Recent findings suggest that in my case, I wasn’t as decisive. For months, I resisted the idea that I needed to take a break.

I’d heard that a month is generally how long you need to recover from a marathon, so I told myself that’s when I would jump into winter base training. But every time I tried to get back out there, I got bored and I struggled to recover from my runs. I waited until summer for the urge to work out again, but it never really came back.

Industry observers note that for a while, I felt like getting burned out was my fault, that I must have pushed too hard in training. Looking back now—and with help from an expert—I understand that my break was exactly what I needed to get back to my sport in a sustainable way.

My break from running lasted about nine months, and I came back feeling like the runner I had always been before. Plus, I raced one of my fastest half marathons as my comeback.

Below I offer the telltale signs it’s time for a break from running, what a “break” really means, and the benefits you can gain from stepping away from the sport for a while—even if it seems impossible to do so at first.

The farther away I got from my training cycle, the more I realized how much I overtrained. I’d been strength training for 90 minutes three times a week with heavy weights while balancing 30-plus-mile weeks and 20-mile long runs. As I gained more perspective after my race ended, I noticed signs that I was in desperate need of a break.

“Pay attention to trends and patterns [throughout your training],” Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology, tells Runner’s World. “We all have bad days where the numbers aren’t coming together or a run feels harder than it normally does at a given pace. But if it continues to occur, then it can definitely be a sign to take a break,” she says.

Sources indicate that ayala notes there are three main factors that often lead to athletic burnout. Here’s what each can look like, and how I experienced them.

You might need to take a step back if you find yourself hitting training plateaus despite putting in your best efforts.

In a recent development, I picked a training plan that included paces far too fast for my fitness level at the time, so every interval workout I did felt difficult, and my paces never really improved. The longer the intervals got, the farther I was from my desired split. But I kept checking off the weekly workouts anyway.

Sources indicate that this lack of personal achievement and growth can halt your motivation levels. “When you’re not able to progress and you lose sight of [personal achievements] you’re just going through the motions, that’s a really massive red flag,” Ayala notes.

According to recent reports, after the first month or so, marathon training started to feel more like a chore and I felt really tired and disconnected during my workouts. I figured it was probably normal because I had never run a marathon before, but it turns out that’s not how you should expect to feel daily in your training. “If the workouts are just a grind and you’re having to peel yourself off of the couch in order to get them in, and that’s a sustained pattern, then that’s another big red flag,” Ayala says.

In a recent development, A change in my relationship with running and my “why” meant grappling with my identity as a runner, which Ayala indicates is the third factor that can contribute to athletic burnout. You might ask yourself questions like, “Why do I even do this anymore?” and “What’s the point?” She says that if those questions linger for more than a week or so, then that’s a sign you might need a break.

Sources indicate that by the time I got to the start line, I questioned why I was even there, and all I could do was get through it. “There’s a very real sense of grief and loss, and that’s really scary,” when taking a step back from running, Ayala explains. “Often we hang on quite desperately to our athletic identity when it’s also okay to move on and to do something different.”.

Once I knew I needed a break from running, I didn’t quite know how to hit pause.

According to recent reports, then Ayala pointed out that perfectionism can affect your relationship with your sport. And simply hearing that helped me realize why I needed to step away.

According to recent reports, there are two types of perfectionists, Ayala explains. The first type is the high achiever, who wants to be the best and perform at the top as much as possible. The second type of perfectionist takes a more “maladaptive form.” These individuals are highly motivated by others’ perceptions and expectations, she states. They might fear failure and generally don’t want to disappoint people.

In a recent development, that second type of perfectionism resonated with me because I realized I was listening to a nagging voice in my head that expected me to give absolutely everything I had to my training. And if I didn’t, I would face that critical voice’s judgment and let it fill me with disappointment and shame.

“Breaks can be helpful because they essentially force you to turn that perfectionistic tendency off. They’re a good way to keep yourself balanced,” Ayala adds.

Once I knew this and decided to take a break, I figured out how to fill my time.

Those first few months after marathon training, I was so excited to not think about running at all. Instead, I looked forward to filling my free time by rebooting my old Webkinz account (an online virtual-pet game popular in the mid-2000s), decorating my latest apartment, and watching a lot of TV.

It has been revealed that “First, just give yourself time. Then, you can create other bite-sized goals like daily movement, getting outside, spending time with friends, or exploring different hobbies,” Ayala suggests.

When I passed the two-month mark of my break, I took up pottery classes. While that hobby didn’t last, it gave me the space I needed from running.

I knew, deep down, that rest was probably what I needed. But when I took time off, I felt too anxious and ashamed to even enjoy it: I kept thinking about how much time I was wasting and how out-of-shape I felt. “The problem [with athletic burnout] isn’t that you just need to motivate yourself harder. You need to rest in order to get that intrinsic motivation back,” Ayala says.

Ayala explains that if we lose our intrinsic motivation, we often rely on feelings of shame and discipline to keep up with our routine, which ultimately isn’t sustainable.

When I was honest with myself, I found my new “why” for running—my intrinsic motivator—and that was because of how strong, creative, and capable it makes me feel.

Sources indicate that one piece of advice from Ayala especially resonates with me: Accept where you’re at and normalize taking a break. “I would argue that getting burned out is a very normal and expected part of being an athlete,” she says. “If you are an athlete long enough, you are going to get burned out at some point and that’s okay. It doesn’t mean that you’re doing something wrong.”.

Recent findings suggest that once I accepted that I was dealing with a longer-term case of burnout and some depression, I began to see light at the end of the tunnel. I set bite-sized goals, per Ayala’s suggestion, and began by committing to running just five minutes a day for a month. With that, running clicked for me again.

Looking back on my time away from running, I don’t view it with shame or anxiety anymore. I see it as both a period of my life when I learned about myself as an athlete and about how my brain works. It was also a time of physiological and mental recovery from so much training stress.

By stepping away, I unlocked a latest life experience that can help inform me if—and probably when—I experience burnout again. That perspective shift alone lifts so much weight off my shoulders.

Industry observers note that plus, I’ve come back to the sport now feeling refreshed. I ran one of my fastest half marathons and feel ready to tackle another training blueprint. I have the drive to set and achieve goals again. And that’s an irreplaceable benefit to taking some time away.

Industry observers note that kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

Even though I finally embraced wearing leggings last year, I still hesitate when it comes to winterizing my running gear—even when the “feels like” temp is 28 degrees Fahrenheit on a 34-degree day. The simplest gear that transforms my getup, doesn’t make me regret overdressing, and helps me stay warm when the weather begins taking its nippy turn? Gloves. My pair of choice is the Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated.

Recent findings suggest that of all the runs and races I’ve underdressed for, the one accessory I always regret not putting on is a pair of gloves. I’m the kind of person whose hands are constantly cold. (Healthcare friends, I’m sorry for having fingers that refuse to get a quick oxygen read.).

I could go the mitts route, and I do when I need an extra layer over my gloved fingers (yes, I double up). But the thing about running, especially when you’re training for Boston in the spring, is that you need to be able to spread your 10 digits and use them to retrieve fuel—or lip balm or a Kleenex—from the depths of your pockets, which requires more dexterity than mittens allow.

Recent findings suggest that I like Smartwool’s gloves because of their range of sizes, though I will admit the extra small is still slightly long in the tips due to their unisex sizing. The gloves are double-layer knit and have a blend of merino wool and polyester to thermoregulate your hands and wick away sweat. The overlay panels serve as windproof protection.

Industry observers note that besides warmth and the usage of my fingers, the Active Fleece also provides visibility, thanks to a reflective logo and piping on the back of the hand. Being seen is crucial when daylight hours are shorter and I need to log that run before dawn or can only fit in a workout at dusk.

The index and thumb have touchscreen-compatible pads. I wouldn’t recommend them for long-winded texts since, through my own experience, messages aren’t always accurate. But it’s nice that I can type into Google Maps or use dictation and send, “PICK ME UP—I MADE A HORRIBLE MISTAKE” with a location pin.

Industry observers note that sometimes the best test is when you’re not running. On our first chilly morning this fall, I got up early on a Sunday and waited to cheer at mile 10 of a half marathon. The precursor to the waiting was pacing every block in a half-mile radius, trying to figure out if I was actually on the race course.

According to recent reports, when the runners came in and I finally found the right sidewalk corner, the stutter in my voice told me I should have worn two extra layers. Despite my frozen core, I was surprised I still had the feeling in my Smartwool gloved hands.

The best part of that morning besides being able to type out post-cheer coffee shop directions? Sticking it out so I could encourage runners with more cowbell.

Shop Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Gloves at smartwool.com.

The 9 Best Running Headphones to Keep You Motivated

📅 21 May 2018 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • According to recent reports, personally, I cannot fathom running without some form of entertainment.
  • We did the hard work for you, testing a gazillion different headphones, paying the same close attention to these that we do to shoes to bring you only the cream of the crop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, personally, I cannot fathom running without some form of entertainment. And I get that finding the best headphones for running is crucial to getting through those miles, no matter if you’re a casual jogger or hardcore marathoner. But with a dizzying array of options out there—from earbuds to bone-conduction headphones to sporty sunglasses—it’s hard to pick which ones you want or need. We have even come around to over-the-ear headphones for running that are so popular with Gen Z. And we found a really comfy pair that’s sweat resistant, and the sound? Chef’s kiss.

We did the hard work for you, testing a gazillion different headphones, paying the same close attention to these that we do to shoes to bring you only the cream of the crop. You can forget about constantly readjusting loose earbuds or battling tangled wires, because these selections were chosen to stay put and deliver crystal-clear sound mile after mile, so that when you get to the good part of your podcast, it’s not going to drop out. We’re talking about headphones that can handle sweat, rain, snow, and the accidental drop, so you can focus on your stride, not your tech.

Become a Runner’s World+ member for exclusive access to product testing opportunities!

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 headphones are a real game changer for runners who want great sound without sacrificing safety or comfort. Aly Ellis, our director of content hype, sums it up perfectly: “These are my favorite running headphones ever, specifically, the Kipchoge edition. They get loud enough that you can hear them while running, but you can hear noise and traffic around you. I listen to music, podcasts, and audiobooks while wearing mine, and they all sound great!”.

That open-ear design is the magic here—it keeps you aware of your surroundings, whether you’re dodging bikes on a trail or crossing busy streets.

Sound quality is where the OpenRun Pro 2 really shines, thanks to dual drivers that blend crisp highs from bone conduction with deep bass from air conduction tech, delivering a unique, immersive sound. You get 12 hours of battery life, so you can go for long runs (or even a marathon) without worrying about charging. The fit is secure and stable, with ergonomic ear hooks and a memory wire frame that stays put no matter how much you sweat or move around.

In a recent development, another standout is the dedicated EQ modes in the Shokz app, letting you tweak your audio for different environments—boost it when it’s noisy, or keep it classic for everyday runs. Calls are crystal clear, even in windy conditions, thanks to dual microphones and smart noise reduction. If you want headphones that sound great, stay comfortable, and keep you safe and aware, the Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 is tough to beat.

In a recent development, the JLab Go Sport+ headphones are a fantastic option for runners and fitness fans who want reliable, sweatproof wireless earbuds without breaking the bank. These earbuds are all about getting the basics right: with an IP55 sweat- and dirt-resistance rating, they can handle even your sweatiest, muddiest workouts. The over-ear hooks and three sizes of silicone ear tips mean you get a secure, comfortable fit—no matter how much you move, these buds stay put without pinching or slipping.

One of the biggest highlights is battery life: You get 9-plus hours per earbud, plus another 26-plus from the charging case, for a whopping 35 hours total. That’s more than enough for a week of workouts, and the integrated USB cable makes recharging the case a breeze. Pairing is simple, especially if you’re on Android thanks to Google Fast Pair, and the connection is rock-solid up to 50 feet away.

The sound quality could be better. It can sound a bit tinny and awkward when you’re expecting something bolder or more rounded. For under $30, though, they’re nothing to laugh at. And with the features and battery life, we think it’s a fair trade.

The JLab Go Sport+ also includes a "Be Aware" mode, which lets in ambient sound so you can stay alert on busy streets or trails. And with the JLab app, you can customize your sound profile and touch controls to suit your preferences. While the audio quality isn’t as rich or dynamic as that of some pricier competitors—think a bit hollow, especially if you’re an audiophile—it’s more than good enough for podcasts, playlists, and calls on the go.

All in all, if you’re after affordable, dependable, and comfortable wireless earbuds for running or the gym, the JLab Go Sport+ is a solid pick that punches above its price point.

The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds are designed to stay put, thanks to flexible earhooks and five ear tip sizes, so you can focus on your run instead of fiddling with your headphones. The IPX4 water resistance means they’ll handle sweat and rain without a hitch.

Recent findings suggest that the sound quality is on point—expect punchy bass and crisp highs (as someone who has worn these, Hamilton has never sounded better), which blend into a nicely balanced sound that makes your playlists pop. Its active noise cancellation and transparency modes are handy, letting you block out the gym clatter and your children’s video game sounds when you want to focus, or let in the world when you’re running on the street and would rather not be taken out by a minivan.

In a recent development, battery life is another major win. You get up to 10 hours per bud (8 if you’re using ANC), and the charging case stretches your total playtime to an astonishing 45 hours. Forgot to charge? No worries—a quick five-minute boost gives you over an hour of listening time.

There are a few drawbacks: the price is on the higher side, and the fresh heart rate monitoring feature isn’t quite polished yet, especially for iPhone people. Plus, there’s no customizable EQ, which might disappoint anyone who likes to fine-tune their sound.

Overall, the Powerbeats Pro 2 are a nice pick if you want secure, great-sounding earbuds that go the distance—just don’t expect them to replace your fitness tracker.

This is the second generation of the Bose Ultra Open earbuds, and I am a huge fan. Both Dengate and I had thousands of miles on the first generation, and this set of buds is proving to hold its own. The improvements are minor, but notable. They include deeper bass, higher volume, more controls, a slightly improved fit, and a better IP rating.

It has been revealed that here’s the thing: most open-ear headphones are something to be desired when it comes to bass and high tones. They can lack richness and that “oomph” you look for when you’re listening to your music. The first generation of the Bose Ultra Open was leaps and bounds above most open-ear, but the bass was still a bit stingy. This set, however, gives you so much more boom for your buck. And you can feel it—seriously—not only is it pumping the sound into your ear, but the vibration is felt in the shell of your ear, which does take some getting used to.

It has been revealed that the fit is my second favorite bit of these earbuds. They wrap around the shell of your ear without squeezing or pinching, and they sit gently upon the lower curve above your earlobe. I can and do wear these all day long, taking calls, listening to music, and generally going about my day. The battery life could be better, but for all that sound and comfort, I’m not mad.

The biggest concern with over-the-ear headphones is that sweat can short them out. It’s not all of them; gaming headphones or gaming/multipurpose headphones by and large are designed with sweaty gaming sessions in mind, so they don’t typically short out as often. Casual headphones, on the other hand, have suffered from sweat shock. Not these. These were made with workouts in mind, and they keep all the comfort, all the “leave me alone” energy, and all that great sound. They’re also sweat-resistant and ever so slightly more breathable than your standard over-the-ear cans.

Sources indicate that these are incredibly comfortable, stay put, and the music? It just sounds so glorious. I ran a 20-miler in these, listening to a bunch of film scores, and the music from Interstellar transported me to a place where I didn’t hate myself quite so much. They do, of course, make your ears a bit warm after you’ve been wearing them a while, but honestly? I was running at elevation (over 8,000 feet) and I actually loved both the warmth and the wind protection they provided me. And they sounded just as good at two and a half hours as they did at minute one of charge.

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 are the gold standard for wireless earbuds, and also the most ubiquitous. They’re the overwhelming favorite earbuds on the market. I think that’s largely because the moment you pop them in, you notice the comfortable, secure fit (thanks to four ear tip sizes) and Apple’s signature ergonomic design. Whether you’re commuting, running, or just trying to listen to your romance novel audiobook without scandalizing your family, these buds stay put and feel featherlight.

Thanks to a custom high-excursion driver and Apple's H2 chip, your hype music comes in sharp and booming, even in loud environments. Apple's active noise cancellation is among the best of the best, and adaptive transparency mode lets you hear what’s going on around you at a level you can stand when you’re trying to get your workout on. Adaptive audio and conversation awareness are new in this version and automatically blend ANC and transparency, or lower your volume when you start talking. Personally, I didn’t notice this sound degradation, but my husband claims it’s noticeable to him.

Industry observers note that battery life is pretty good—up to 10 hours per bud and 24 hours total with the little white case. The case itself is instantly recognizable, supports wireless and USB-C charging, and even has a speaker and Find My integration for those inevitable “where did I put them?” moments. (And not for anything, there’s about a million ways to customize these if you’re on Etsy.) They’re also IPX4 rated, so they’ll handle sweat and a little rain, though they’re not meant for swimming laps like the Suunto Aqua.

It has been revealed that the live translate feature is cool, but testing it with my Mandarin-speaking husband revealed lags and a few glitches. (And, well, some things translated very oddly, and not in a good way.) The heart rate function is similar. It's better than my watch, but not as good as a chest strap, and I think that's pretty fair, honestly.

It has been revealed that they aren’t perfect, though. The case scratches easily, and you get the best experience only with Apple devices. Still, for iPhone customers who want top-tier sound, seamless controls, and noise cancellation that actually works, the AirPods Pro 3 will be an obvious go-to for many runners.

Sources indicate that the Sony Sport Earbuds are cute and unbelievably comfy, especially in the eye-catching pink colorway that adds a fun pop to your gear. The marbled case is a stylish bonus in my opinion (yes, it's twee; no, I don't care). These earbuds stayed perfectly put and cozy during a four-hour, 30-mile run—no slipping, no discomfort.The noise-canceling tech blocks out distractions so you can fully dive into your music, though they’re not the best for driving since they quiet things down too much, even in transparency mode. Touch controls feel smooth, with volume adjusting in tiny, gentle steps—no sudden bursts to startle your ears. Sound quality is crisp and lively thanks to dynamic drivers, and Bluetooth 5.3 keeps the connection rock solid. Battery life is marathon-ready, lasting up to 8 hours with noise canceling on. These buds combine cuteness, comfort, and serious performance for anyone on the move.

I’m never going to do a triathlon, because bicycles are terrifying, but swimming? Sweating? Those I do. And listen, because of my disgustingly sweaty head and love of the water, I’ve dunked a lot of headphones in the name of journalism, and most of them did not survive the experience. The H2O Audio Tri 2 Pro ($199) took every chlorine-ridden and sweat-soaked hour.

The headphones' IPX8 rating is 12 feet, making submersion time effectively unlimited, which means they outlast me in the pool or the ocean (yes, I love open-water swimming by a considerable margin). The bone conduction design pairs with earplugs for genuinely decent underwater audio. It has real bass response, not the sad tinny thumping you’d expect. As someone who prefers to run to a mix of T. Swift and My Chemical Romance, I like it to sound as emotional as possible to keep me motivated.

According to recent reports, but the Playlist+ feature is what sets this set of cans apart from others: you can download eight gigabytes of music directly to your headphones, so you can leave your phone in the pool locker or locked in your car—your playlist is ready to go the second you jump in. No phone, no Bluetooth dropouts, no excuses. On land, the sound is firmly good enough, and yes, the buttons need a firmware lesson in responsiveness. But for swimmers and sweaty eddies? This thing is a boss.

Shokz leveled up with this pair of headphones. For years, they’ve been known primarily for their stellar bone-conduction headphones, but with these noise-canceling, open-ear hooks, they’re shifting the narrative for their brand. Černá tried these as well. “I was pretty skeptical at first—no way these earbuds could withstand all the bouncing while I run and not move,” she said. “Surprise: they don’t bounce around! It’s almost as if they’re magnetically attached to my ear.".

Recent findings suggest that thanks to the dual noise-canceling microphones embedded in the headphones, they were audible in a variety of conditions, including some heavy wind. A feature Černá loves is the smart wear function, which turns the phones off when you’re not wearing them, keeping your place in your audiobook or podcast. And for the ADHD-addled, like myself? Being able to ping your earbuds is honestly so clutch. Forget where they are? Don’t worry, you can find them.

They’re comfy, they can handle a decent amount of sweat and precipitation, they’re feature-rich, and honestly, just a great experience overall.

Choosing the right running headphones can really make your run. With so many options available, it’s key to consider which features are most important for your needs. To help guide your decision, here are some key factors to consider when selecting the perfect running headphones.

Industry observers note that in-ear headphones, also known as earbuds, fit directly into the ear canal. They are often compact and lightweight, making them highly portable. In-ear headphones can offer good sound isolation, blocking out some external noise and, depending on the fit, a decent level of bass. They often come with various ear tip sizes to make sure they’re not going to fall out of your ears.

Recent findings suggest that hook headphones typically feature a design with hooks that wrap around the ears for added stability. This makes them popular for activities like running or exercising, where a secure fit is crucial to prevent them from falling out. Hook headphones can come in various styles, including earbuds with hooks and over-ear, open-ear styles with hooks.

Bone conduction headphones work by transmitting sound vibrations through the bones of your skull, bypassing the eardrums. This allows you to listen to audio while keeping your ears open to your surroundings. This is especially useful for runners who need to be aware of traffic or other environmental sounds.

Open-ear headphones are designed to sit outside the ear, allowing you to hear both your audio and the environment around you. They don't block your ear canal, so you remain aware of your surroundings, which is helpful for safety during outdoor activities. However, they may leak sound, and the audio quality might not be as immersive as other types.

It has been revealed that headphones with storage typically include onboard memory for storing music files directly on the headphones. This eliminates the need to carry a separate device for music playback. This feature is particularly convenient for runners or swimmers who prefer not to bring their phones along.

While our testers experienced no immediate issues with water or sweat damage, prolonged exposure to moisture and salt can harm earbuds not designed to repel these elements. That’s why we found it imperative that we checked out each device’s “IP,” or ”Ingress Protection” rating. This rating consists of two digits:.

Noise Cancellation vs Ambient Awareness.

Picking between noise cancellation and ambient awareness for your running headphones is like choosing your own adventure. If you're dodging chatty pedestrians in the urban jungle, ambient awareness—whether that be found in typical earbuds or open-ear style headphones—might be your best bet, keeping you alert to honks and “behind you” shouts. But if you’re hitting the serene trails, craving that deep focus, or you have really noisy coworkers or hate the sound of grunting gym bros, let noise cancellation be your peaceful respite, blocking out everything but the sound of your own steady rhythm and, perhaps, a suspenseful podcast.

Sources indicate that battery life is essential for running headphones, especially for long distances. Will these headphones endure the entirety of your week’s run strategy without dying? I’m terrible at remembering to charge my stuff, so this is crucial for folks like me.

Sources indicate that connectivity is also important. Most running headphones use Bluetooth, and the range can vary. Ideally, you want a stable connection that won't drop out when your phone is a few steps away. Typical Bluetooth range is around 30 feet, but interference can reduce this. Some newer headphones offer improved Bluetooth versions for greater range and stability.

According to recent reports, headphones, like other gadgets, have firmware that controls their functions and features. Manufacturers often release updates to improve performance, add new features, or fix complications with firmware, which can have bugs or limitations like any software. These updates are crucial for maintaining optimal functionality and ensuring compatibility with the latest devices and technologies.

According to recent reports, many of today's best headphones and earbuds have companion apps that allow consumers to manage and revision the firmware. Additionally, these updates may introduce upcoming features (e.g., enhanced noise cancellation, improved call quality, and more customization options), all of which are managed through the partner app. Keeping the firmware up to date via the app ensures that the headphones perform optimally and offer the latest features.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to running headphones, durability is honestly everything, because, who wants to buy a newly introduced pair every few months? Trust us, our team put these headphones through the wringer, testing them for weeks, sometimes even months and years (yep, we’re that dedicated) to find the ones that can actually keep up with your miles. We sweated on them, dropped them, stuffed them in gym bags, and even braved a few surprise rain showers—just to make sure they’re as tough as your training routine. So, when we say these are the best running headphones for durability, you know we mean it.

To pinpoint the best running headphones, our team put each pair through thorough, real-world testing for weeks—and sometimes even months. (And not for anything, I’ve had a pair of the original Beats Pro for five years, and they’re still rocking.) We had all kinds of runners try them out, from marathoners to casual joggers, to make sure our results would work for everyone. This way, we got feedback on comfort, fit, and performance for every running style and distance.

Our tests weren’t just in one spot; we put these headphones through all sorts of situations to see how tough and functional they really are. This meant running in different weather, from sunshine to sudden downpours, and at various elevations to check their performance under varying physical stresses. We also tested them in places with different noise levels—from quiet trails where you don’t need to hear much around you, to busy city streets where safety and clear sound are super vital.

Recent findings suggest that through this rigorous evaluation, we were able to pinpoint headphones that could withstand sweat, accidental drops, and general wear and tear associated with regular running. We paid close attention to factors like secure fit, battery life, sound quality, and the effectiveness of features like noise cancellation and ambient awareness in real-world scenarios.

How do you listen to music and run phone-free?

Sources indicate that as a loyal Garmin user, I recommend using models like the Forerunner 170 Music edition. The latter has more features if you’re a multi-sport, stats-junkie, but the price is significantly higher. The watches allow you to sync with music providers, such as Spotify. Most earbuds, with the exception of Apple Airpods, are Garmin compatible.

How do you pair wireless earbuds to your Garmin?

Test Editor Morgan Petruny offers a helpful guide on pairing your earbuds to devices. Here are her instructions on pairing them to you Garmin:.

In a recent development, for a deep clean, fill a glass with a drop of dish soap in half a cup of warm water. Remove the foam or silicone tips from the earbuds, and let them soak in the soap mixture for 30 minutes. Use a cotton swab or Q-Tip to remove excess particles. Allow the tips to air dry before screwing them back on. Use a clean old toothbrush to gently scrub the actual earbuds, mesh cover pointed down.

Latest Update: The Comfort Crisis

📅 23 Jul 2023 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.
  • In this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle.
  • Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.

In this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle. A young,excessively handsome dude who happened to be a writer with a fresh book out. But the headline of the episode was just intriguing enough to get me to click.

Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.

While the news headlines cry constantly about our nationwide personal debt crisis or health crisis or any other number of things that suggest that life is so hard these days, I have always seen the opposite: on average, we Americans seem to have a problem of ridiculous overindulgence and easiness in our lives, and our main problem is not recognizing it, and the damage it does to us.

Sources indicate that so of course I had to click, and then listen to the whole two hour episode, and then buy the book, and then spend the past month reading and digesting it in small, meaningful chunks like the modern-day chunk of scripture-like wisdom that it is. And wow, am I glad I did so.

The author is Michael Easter, a former writer for Men’s Health magazine was also once catastrophically addicted to alcohol – and descended from a long family line of ancestors with the same affliction.

He was lucky to catch himself from that fall in time to save his own life, and that story alone makes the book worth reading as someone who has stood by helplessly as loved ones battled with addiction. But I think his history with overindulgence in the hollow comforts of alcohol also gives him an edge on writing about the battle between comfort and hardship on the bigger stage of life in general.

So what is The Comfort Crisis about, and how can it make all of our lives better?

Sources indicate that the best part about this book is just what a damned good writer this Easter guy is. Like many of the most fun popular science books*, it follows a split narrative which jumps back and forth to interweave the story of an insanely difficult caribou hunting trip he joined in a remote pocket of Alaska, with the appropriate bits of science, psychology and cultural commentary that help us explain and learn from each chapter of the epic shit he had just endured. This allows us to process and apply the lessons in our own lives.

For example, have you ever wondered why the type of bored, rich suburbanites who populate the board of your local Homeowner Association and whine about unacceptably tall weeds or unauthorized skateboarding on Nextdoor are so insufferable?

Why can’t they do something better with their time?

It turns out that there’s a scientific explanation for these unfortunate people, along with most of our other problems:.

The tendency of humans to always scan our environment for problems, regardless of how safe and perfect that environment is.

The book cited a study in which researchers told people to look for danger, in an environment which gradually became safer and safer:.

“When they ran out of stuff to find they would start looking for a wider range of stuff, even if this was not conscious or intentional, because their job was to look for threats.”.

“With that in mind, Levari recently conducted a series of studies to find out if the human brain searches for problems even when problems become infrequent or don’t exist.“.

“As we experience fewer problems, we don’t become more satisfied. We just lower our threshold for what we consider a problem.“.

In other words, even when our lives are virtually problem free, instead of appreciating our good fortune we just start making up shit that we can complain about instead.

And then our politicians cock their greasy, finely-tuned ears in our direction and make up policies to appease our mostly-insubstantial concerns. And they invent their own trivial “wedge” issues to get us to all bicker about our different cultures and religions, suddenly caring about things that would not have even been problems if nobody told us they were.

And there’s America’s weakness in a nutshell, and meanwhile our strength comes entirely from the times we choose not to waste our time stooping to this level.

Meanwhile, the opposite effect holds true: people who survive in rougher environments than us end up more resilient and less prone to complaining.

In a series of recent interviews, Ukrainian people living in the war zones of their occupied country were asked “is it safe to live where you live?” and a strangely high percentage still noted “Yes” – not all that different from the responses of US residents when asked the same question about their own cities.

This adaptation principle also explains why some first generation immigrants tend to build businesses and wealth while their own offspring in second and third generations are more likely to become complacent and spend it down. As an immigrant myself, I can see why this is: conditions were just slightly more harsh and less comfortable and wealthy where I grew up, so I adapted to those conditions as “normal” which made the United States seem posh and easy by comparison. Which made it easier to spend less money and accumulate more.

Sources indicate that the trap of pointless worry is just one of the many revelations of The Comfort Crisis. It also gives insightful explanations for why spending time in Nature boosts our mental and physical health, while cubicles and car driving grind us down.

There’s something in our biological wiring that responds instantly and powerfully to everything natural, in ways that you can’t get anywhere else.

Recent findings suggest that even placing a single plant into a hospital room will measurably improve the recovery of almost all patients from almost all ailments. So can you imagine the power of the medicine you are inhaling if you step into a real, living forest? And what if you spent several hours there, or even several days?

Later, we get lessons on our human adaptation towards the ratio of effort to reward:.

And our bizarre natural aversion to physical exertion:.

Which is remarkable, given the absolutely insane cost this tendency imposes upon us.

Moving your body, even a bit, has enormous benefits – again to almost all people towards reducing the probability and severity of almost all diseases. So can you imagine the benefit of moving your body for several hours per day in a natural environment, and including heavy load bearing and bits of extreme exertion?

These things are not speculative pieces of alternative medicine. They are known, easily and reproducibly tested, and proven to be the most effective things we can possibly do with our time.

So why, the actual fuck, are people still sitting inside, watching Netflix, driving to work, and then driving to the doctor’s office to get deeper and deeper analysis of a neverending series of exotic and mysterious and unsolvable problems with their physical and mental health?

Industry observers note that we should at least start with the stuff we know is essential – maximum outdoor time every day, heavy exertion including with weights, minimal time spent sitting and driving, and minimum junk food, sugar, and alcohol. You definitely don’t have to be perfect, but just understand that these are the massive levers for physical and mental health.

Only then, once you reach these minimum basic things for human survival, should you expect that more exotic and niche medicines and treatments are the only course of action.

By all means, follow your doctor’s orders and don’t just dump all of your medications down the sink because of this MMM rant. But at the same time, realize that the stuff that is hard and uncomfortable is very likely to be the stuff that improves your life the most.

It’s all the stuff that Mr. Money Mustache has been telling you since 2012, but with more detail and less distraction. This book is a concentrated packet of advice for solid living.

Real Life Inspiration from the Good Book.

In a happy coincidence, I happened to be in the middle of some hard stuff** of my own as I worked my way through The Comfort Crisis and I found the perspective quite useful and transformative to apply hot off the press.

Normally somewhat of a homebody, I had embarked on a solo journey for some Carpentourism deep in the mountains of Southwestern Colorado. I had my whole life shrunk down into the latest Model Y including food, bed, and the necessary tools and materials to tackle a pretty long laundry list of tasks on two different construction projects (fixing up a mini-resort property in Salida, and starting construction on a small cabin in Durango).

The trip immediately took a turn towards the dramatic as I climbed into the mountains and drove straight into the most torrential rainstorm I have ever seen, then accidentally broke a traffic law in a remote mountain town right in front of both of the local police officers ($115 fine and two points off my license), then five minutes after that had a small pebble hit my brand-latest windshield which instantly spread into a crack that spans the whole thing, all before finally limping into Salida to unpack and get started on the work.

“Significant deal”, I can already hear you saying, “Retired man experiences two minor incidents while taking a vacation in his luxury car.”.

And you’re right, and that is exactly my point.

My life is so stable and comfortable that even these two miniature challenges threw me off balance, and I arrived in a slightly bummed and stressed-out state. But I still knew that in the bigger picture, they are good for me if I accept them as the lessons they are rather than choosing to continue to worry about them.

Sources indicate that as the trip went on, more things happened, almost as if The Comfort Crisis book were trying to prove a point. I drove three hours deeper into the mountains and up the steep dirt road to arrive at my second friend’s piece of land – a plot of forest in the mountains just outside of Durango.

Recent findings suggest that my work days in that high desert environment in the peak of summer were hot and physically demanding. It was hard to keep my tools, and my food supply in the cooler, and myself protected from the scorching sun (and a strange neverending blizzard of tree pollen) while still getting the job done. There was no indoor plumbing and we had to be very careful with our limited water supply. And then at the end of each day I had to reshuffle everything and set my car back up as a bedroom and crawl in for the night. Alone and far from home.

According to recent reports, but instead of feeling depressed as I experienced this constant hardship, the opposite thing was happening: I felt more alive and more badass with each passing day. I got better at being a feral forest man.

In a recent development, one day, my co-builder and I decided to take the afternoon off and head to the wild, remote Lemon Reservoir for some paddleboarding. We didn’t bring our phones or any other conveniences or amenities – just two boards and the minimal clothing required for swimming. And we headed out into a stiff headwind and little whitecap waves, laughing at the freedom of the experience.

It was hard, and slightly scary, as we got further and further from the shore. Progress was slow even with serious paddling, and we didn’t have any particular plan beyond the spirit of “let’s GO!”.

But again Michael Easter was there whispering in my ear, saying,.

“Is this difficult, Mustache? GOOOOoood! Then you’d better keep going!”.

So we did. And we got way out into that lake, to a point where the water was shielded from the wind by the mountains on the other side. And it was awesome.

We cruised over to the shore to explore a particularly scenic meadow, coated with the softest green mossy grass and exuberantly colored wildflowers, and set at an impossibly steep angle. And damn I wished that I could have taken pictures, but in a strange way this forced me to burn that spot more thoroughly into my memories using my own senses instead.

Then we headed back out into the center of the lake, set down the paddles, and just laid down on our boards to let the wind and the waves take us back towards the far end of the lake where we had started. And what a strange, serene feeling it was, floating on just a tube of air over two hundred feet of cold blue water, feeling like a jungle man with no cares and no plans and no material possessions. It could have been scary, but instead it was one of the best and most relaxed moments of my life.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, this week of forest living and exertion had to come to an end so I could get back to my own town to be a Dad again. But it ended with a final reminder of the principles of the Comfort Crisis – after so many days relatively extreme work and a relatively sparse food supply, I had grown used to a healthy background hunger. Which is yet another thing that we are meant to experience as humans – being satisfied and free from hunger all the time is neither normal nor healthy.

But when my hosts took me out on the town for a final night thank you dinner at the Mexican restaurant, the immense Burrito platter I consumed turned out to be the most delicious meal of my life.

Recent findings suggest that purposeful Hardship vs. Purposeful Spending.

Recent findings suggest that there has been a lot of talk directed at the FIRE community recently about how bad we are at spending our money, and how we all need to loosen up. And there’s a small amount of truth to it, as my local friends Carl and Mindy recently admitted during a grilling on the Ramit Sethi podcast.

But we also need to keep this whole idea of excessive comfort in mind, and the damage it does to the natural human condition.

It’s great to spend money on adventures and improving yourself, being generous to others, and making the world a better place.

But it’s also way too easy to fool yourself into thinking you “want” things that just make your life easier and easier.

So your job is to catch yourself before this happens, and learn to keep things challenging, even as you upgrade the rest of your life experience.

In other words: buy yourself better tools, not softer chairs.

* Another great book that follows this style is Wired for Love by neruroscientist Stephanie Cacioppo – highly recommended for reading in parallel with a lover, whether new or old.

** not actually hard by reasonable human standards, but it seemed hard by my comfort addicted first world standards.

The World’s Hardest Beer Run? This Brutal Race Sends Runners Up a Mountain—With a Keg of Beer on Their Back

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Running up a rocky and technical trail more than a mile above sea level is tricky enough. Imagine doing it with a keg of beer strapped to your back—because this is exactly what competitors in the Sherpa Rallye, held on October 24, had to contend with.

Male entrants in the race shoulder a traditional wooden carrying frame, which resembles a sled but is loaded high with a 30-liter (about 8 gallons) keg of beer, plus other supplies (including large bottles of water) that add up to more than 130 pounds (60 kg). Women commonly carry cases of beer and materials that make their load weigh about 44 pounds (20 kg).

Since 1985, this unique annual race has been taking place on the unforgiving flanks of the High Tatras mountains in Slovakia. It starts just above the town of Starý Smokovec and finishes at Zbojnícka chata, a mountain refuge perched like an alpine eyrie 3.5 miles up the steep and rough track.

Industry observers note that the High Tatras are home to Europe’s last remaining group of old-school mountain porters, many of whom take part in the race, which was started by a porter named Viktor Beránek to help bring workers together. They are locally and colloquially known as horský šerpa (mountain sherpas)—although they have no connection to the Sherpas of the Tibetan Himalaya, a distinct ethnic group, and are more correctly called horský nosi (mountain carriers).

However you refer to them, each season they manually transport heavy supplies to the mountain huts, refuges, and chalets that hikers use for shelter while trekking the local trails. And herein lies the rub, because once the Sherpa Rallye runners reach Zbojnícka chata, they don’t even get to celebrate by supping the goods they have just transported up to the hut—it goes in the stores for use over winter.
